extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of the history of philosophy and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook-style account comparing Greek and oriental philosophies, assessing authors (Plato, Aristotle, Lucian, Marcus Aurelius, etc.) and tracing cultural influence on religion, art, and morals. Aimed to explain historical significance and intellectual character across authors and schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance of style / Attic wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'true elegance of Greek style, and the spirit of the Attic wit' as a positive literary quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are valued for clarity, elegance, and Attic wit; e.g., Lucian retains this elegance. Anti-pattern: prose lacking elegance or Attic sensibility is implicitly devalued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraits or 'pictures' of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of an author to present vivid 'pictures of manners' is highlighted as a central value (Lucian's 'highest value... consists... in his pictures of manners').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that give lively, accurate depictions of social character and manners are prized. Example: Lucian as a model. Anti-pattern: abstract or purely doctrinal writing that neglects human character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful and unaffected style
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'beautiful and unaffected style' is singled out as a merit in historians (e.g., Arrian placed near Xenophon for this quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical writing should aim for natural, unaffected expression rather than ornate or forced rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical acquaintance and depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an author's works exhibit 'perfect acquaintance' with a philosophical school (e.g., Marcus Aurelius' meditation's 'perfect acquaintance with the philosophy of the Stoics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authors by their fidelity to and understanding of philosophical doctrines. Shallow or superficial treatment of a school's ideas is a shortcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, precision, and intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and precision in exposition are important; lack of these (Plato sometimes 'dark and sophistical', Aristotle 'obscurity') is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: clear, well-defined limits and precise conceptions. Anti-patterns: 'ill-defined limits', 'dark hints', 'unintelligible formulas' — these reduce philosophical value and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of dialectic: negative vs positive parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's dialectic is described as 'only the negative' (combating error), whereas his positive teaching is expressed by 'emblems, and fables, and poetical mysteries'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a philosopher uses dialectic primarily to refute (negative) or to reveal (positive), and whether their positive mode (allegory/mystery) aids or obscures understanding. Anti-pattern: overreliance on enigmatic allegory without clear doctrinal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inspiration/mysticism vs reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's attribution of knowledge to 'higher and supernatural sources' and inspiration is contrasted with those who rely on reason/experience only (Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments hinge on epistemological stance: mystical/supernatural claims may yield sublime insights but risk vagueness; strict rationalism yields system and method but may fail on 'high questions'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific form versus artistic contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato 'treated of philosophy altogether as an art' while 'Aristotle as a science'; Plato = model of Greek art, Aristotle = model of Grecian science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess philosophical works for orientation toward aesthetic, contemplative expression versus systematic, scientific inquiry. Both have strengths: art for inspiration and beauty, science for rigor and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic completeness and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophies are judged by whether they form a complete, consistent system (Plato's philosophy described as 'essentially incomplete'; Aristotle gives many 'separate inquiries' but lacks a coherent exposition of the universe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference given to philosophies that offer consistent rules of thinking and coherent systems; piecemeal or fragmentary systems are critiqued as insufficient for 'the whole life of man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation between reason and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's method attempts to reconcile reason and experience through 'intermediate contrivances' (e.g., ether world), and his approach is judged on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether proposed mediating hypotheses are inventive and useful or lead to unsatisfactory 'empty formulas' and abstractions. Anti-pattern: contrivances that obscure rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conception: virtue as mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's ethical principle: virtue defined as 'the middle point between two extremes' and moral evil as 'either too much or too little'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mean-as-virtue criterion to assess ethical systems; systems that lack practical measures or that reduce ethics to formula without guidance risk being unsatisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to mysticism among followers
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of later followers (e.g., New-Platonists) to fall 'into the extreme of mysticism and enthusiasm' as a consequence of their master's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating schools, consider how original doctrines may be amplified into mysticism by disciples; warn against unchecked mystic developments that depart from earlier rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of oriental opinions and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of 'oriental opinions and principles' (Egyptian, Persian, Indian sources) altered Greek thought and produced 'wilder superstitions' alongside access to 'old and pure fountains of truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural synthesis in philosophical systems: it can enrich (recover sublime conceptions) or corrupt (introduce superstition). Evaluate both provenance and critical assimilation of foreign elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cultural significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest between Christianity and heathen philosophy is framed as a central 'intellectual contest' that is the 'keystone upon which everything hangs' in cultural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure works by their broader influence on language, art, morals, and the fate of nations; historical impact is an important evaluative dimension beyond internal philosophical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to sources / historical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Value placed on grounding claims in 'monuments and testimonies of antiquity' and on careful treatment of origins (e.g., Mosaic account as 'foundation of all historical truth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical-philosophical claims by their evidentiary support and critical handling of sources; speculative or chronologically implausible assertions are critiqued as 'palpably fabulous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with moral/religious doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a philosophical system harmonizes or conflicts with religious doctrines (Mosaic and Christian revelations considered central reference points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems for alignment or dissonance with prevailing moral/religious frameworks; their capacity to support a 'rule and standard for the whole life of man' is part of their worth.
